title: Partial Derivatives
lead: A partial derivative differentiates a function of several variables with respect to one of them while the others are held constant, and on a graph it is the slope of a tangent line parallel to an axis. This section computes partial derivatives from the definition and by the rules, goes on to higher-order and mixed partial derivatives, and meets the partial differential equations of heat, waves and Laplace.
objectives: Calculate the partial derivatives of a function of two variables.
Calculate the partial derivatives of a function of more than two variables.
Determine the higher-order derivatives of a function of two variables.
Explain the meaning of a partial differential equation and give an example.
summary_html:
• A partial derivative is a derivative involving a function of more than one independent variable.
  • To calculate a partial derivative with respect to a given variable, treat all the other variables as constants and use the usual differentiation rules.
  • Higher-order partial derivatives can be calculated in the same way as higher-order derivatives.

exercises.prompt:
Use a contour map to estimate $\partial f/\partial y$ at point $(0,\sqrt{2})$ for the function

$$f(x,y)=x^{2}-y^{2}.$$

Compare this with the exact answer.

answer.solution: Using the curves corresponding to $c=-2\;\text{and}\;c=-3,$ we obtain ${\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}|}_{(x,y)=(0,\sqrt{2})}\approx \frac{f(0,\sqrt{3})-f(0,\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}}=\frac{-3-(-2)}{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}}=-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}\approx -3.146.$ The exact answer is ${\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}|}_{(x,y)=(0,\sqrt{2})}=({-2y|}_{(x,y)=(0,\sqrt{2})}=-2\sqrt{2}\approx -2.828.$
answer.hint: Create a contour map for $f$ using values of $c$ from $-3\;\text{to}\;3.$ Which of these curves passes through point $(0,\sqrt{2})?$

exercises.prompt:
Use the limit definition of partial derivatives to calculate $\partial f/\partial x$ for the function

$$f(x,y,z)=2x^{2}-4x^{2}y+2y^{2}+5xz^{2}-6x+3z-8.$$

Then find $\partial f/\partial y$ and $\partial f/\partial z$ by setting the other two variables constant and differentiating accordingly.

answer.solution: $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=4x-8xy+5z^{2}-6,\;\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=-4x^{2}+4y,\;\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=10xz+3$
answer.hint: Use the strategy in the preceding example.

exercises.prompt: Calculate $\partial f/\partial x,$ $\partial f/\partial y,$ and $\partial f/\partial z$ for the function $f(x,y,z)=\sec (x^{2}y)-\tan (x^{3}yz^{2}).$

answer.solution: $\begin{array}{l}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2xy\;\sec (x^{2}y)\tan (x^{2}y)-3x^{2}yz^{2}{\sec }^{2}(x^{3}yz^{2}) \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=x^{2}\sec (x^{2}y)\tan (x^{2}y)-x^{3}z^{2}{\sec }^{2}(x^{3}yz^{2}) \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=-2x^{3}yz\;{\sec }^{2}(x^{3}yz^{2})\end{array}$
answer.hint: Use the strategy in the preceding example.

exercises.prompt:
Calculate all four second partial derivatives for the function

$$f(x,y)=\sin (3x-2y)+\cos (x+4y).$$

answer.solution: $\begin{array}{l}\frac{{\partial}^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}=-9\;\sin (3x-2y)-\cos (x+4y) \\ \frac{{\partial}^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}=6\;\sin (3x-2y)-4\;\cos (x+4y) \\ \frac{{\partial}^{2}f}{\partial y\partial x}=6\;\sin (3x-2y)-4\;\cos (x+4y) \\ \frac{{\partial}^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}=-4\;\sin (3x-2y)-16\;\cos (x+4y)\end{array}$
answer.hint: Follow the same steps as in the previous example.

exercises.prompt:
Verify that $u(x,y,t)=2\;\sin (\frac{x}{3})\sin (\frac{y}{4})e^{-25t/16}$ is a solution to the heat equation

$$u_{t}=9(u_{xx}+u_{yy}).\tag{14.21}$$

answer.solution: Differentiate $u=2\sin (\frac{x}{3})\sin (\frac{y}{4})e^{-25t/16}$ one variable at a time, holding the others constant. With respect to $t$: $u_{t}=-\frac{25}{16}\cdot 2\sin (\frac{x}{3})\sin (\frac{y}{4})e^{-25t/16}=-\frac{25}{16}u.$ With respect to $x$ twice: $u_{x}=\frac{2}{3}\cos (\frac{x}{3})\sin (\frac{y}{4})e^{-25t/16}$ and $u_{xx}=-\frac{2}{9}\sin (\frac{x}{3})\sin (\frac{y}{4})e^{-25t/16}=-\frac{1}{9}u.$ With respect to $y$ twice: $u_{yy}=-\frac{1}{16}u.$ Then $9(u_{xx}+u_{yy})=9(-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16})u=9\cdot (-\frac{25}{144})u=-\frac{25}{16}u=u_{t},$ so $u$ satisfies Equation 14.21.
answer.hint: Calculate the partial derivatives and substitute into the right-hand side.

exercises.prompt:
Find the indicated higher-order partial derivatives.

$f_{xy}$ for $z=\ln (x-y)$

Find the indicated higher-order partial derivatives.

Let $z=x^{2}+3xy+2y^{2}.$ Find $\frac{{\partial}^{2}z}{\partial x^{2}}$ and $\frac{{\partial}^{2}z}{\partial y^{2}}.$
Given $f(x,y,z)=xyz,$ find $f_{xyy},f_{yxy},$ and $f_{yyx}.$
Given $f(x,y,z)=e^{-2x}\sin (z^{2}y),$ show that $f_{xyy}=f_{yxy}.$

answer.solution: Hold the other variables constant one at a time. $f_{x}=-2e^{-2x}\sin (z^{2}y),$ so $f_{xy}=-2z^{2}e^{-2x}\cos (z^{2}y)$ and $f_{xyy}=2z^{4}e^{-2x}\sin (z^{2}y).$ In the other order, $f_{y}=z^{2}e^{-2x}\cos (z^{2}y),$ $f_{yx}=-2z^{2}e^{-2x}\cos (z^{2}y)$ and $f_{yxy}=2z^{4}e^{-2x}\sin (z^{2}y).$ The two are equal, $f_{xyy}=f_{yxy}=2z^{4}e^{-2x}\sin (z^{2}y),$ as Clairaut’s theorem extended to higher-order derivatives predicts, since all these partial derivatives are continuous.

The equation for heat flow in the $xy\text{-plane}$ is $\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{{\partial}^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{{\partial}^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}.$ Show that $f(x,y,t)=e^{-2t}\sin x\;\sin y$ is a solution.

answer.solution: With $f(x,y,t)=e^{-2t}\sin x\sin y$: $\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=-2e^{-2t}\sin x\sin y.$ Holding $y$ and $t$ constant, $\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}=-e^{-2t}\sin x\sin y,$ and holding $x$ and $t$ constant, $\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}=-e^{-2t}\sin x\sin y.$ Their sum is $-2e^{-2t}\sin x\sin y=\frac{\partial f}{\partial t},$ so $f$ is a solution of the heat flow equation.

exercises.prompt: The basic wave equation is $f_{tt}=f_{xx}.$ Verify that $f(x,t)=\sin (x+t)$ and $f(x,t)=\sin (x-t)$ are solutions.

answer.solution: For $f(x,t)=\sin (x+t),$ $f_{t}=\cos (x+t)$ and $f_{tt}=-\sin (x+t),$ while $f_{x}=\cos (x+t)$ and $f_{xx}=-\sin (x+t),$ so $f_{tt}=f_{xx}.$ For $f(x,t)=\sin (x-t),$ $f_{t}=-\cos (x-t)$ and $f_{tt}=-\sin (x-t),$ while $f_{xx}=-\sin (x-t),$ so again $f_{tt}=f_{xx}.$ Both are solutions of the wave equation.

A Cobb-Douglas production function is $f(x,y)=200x^{0.7}y^{0.3},$ where $x\;\text{and}\;y$ represent the amount of labor and capital available. Let $x=500$ and $y=1000.$ Find $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at these values, which represent the marginal productivity of labor and capital, respectively.

answer.solution: $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at $(500,1000)=172.36,$ $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ at $(500,1000)=36.93$
